0.title: Decisions, Guidance and the Freedom of a Child
0.essay:
Two offers sit side by side on the kitchen table. Or a person you love asks a question that needs an answer. Or the lease is ending, and you must choose where to live. You pray, and nothing seems to come. You lie awake wondering: what if I choose wrongly, and miss what God wanted for my life? If you know that feeling, this study is for you.

A real ache, and a real question

Christians want to please God. But that good desire can turn into a kind of dread, as if God had hidden one right answer to every choice and were waiting to see whether we would find it.

Scripture speaks to this ache with great tenderness and great clarity. God has not left us to guess. He has told us a great deal about his will. Where he has not spoken, he gives wisdom, the counsel of his people and the freedom of children. And under every choice lies his providence, which carries his people even through their mistakes.

Where we are going

We will name the anxiety, ask what the Bible means by God’s will, weigh the main ways Christians seek guidance, and look at what our hearts are really asking for. Then we will stand in Gethsemane, where Jesus said to his Father, “not my will, but yours” (Luke 22:42), and see what that prayer won for us. We end with practical steps for a real decision, and for the peace that can follow it.

The studies The Providence of God and The Holy Spirit each have a chapter on guidance, and Faith for Young Adults has one on life choices. This study builds on them.

The chapters

Frozen at the Crossroads; The Will God Keeps and the Will God Gives; Blueprints, Fleeces and Lots; What Lies Beneath; Not My Will, but Yours; and Making the Decision, and Afterwards.

For reflection

What decision is on your mind as you begin this study? When you think about “God’s will” for it, do you feel peace, pressure or fear?

1.title: Frozen at the Crossroads
1.essay:
It might be a job, a marriage, a move to another city, a new church or a course of study. The choice is real and the stakes feel high. You make lists. You pray. You ask friends, then ask them again. And underneath it all runs one fear: what if I get this wrong, and miss God’s will for my life?

What it feels like

For some people the anxiety is quiet: a constant hum of uncertainty that follows them for weeks. For others it is loud: sleepless nights, a knot in the stomach, the same arguments going round and round. Every option seems to have a shadow. If I take the job, I may regret leaving my church. If I stay, I may be refusing a door God opened. If I marry, what if there was someone else? If I do not, what if this was the one?

Many Christians carry a picture they have never put into words. Somewhere, they imagine, God has drawn a single right line through their life: one right course, one right town, one right spouse. Their task is to find that line and stay on it. Step off it once, and they will spend the rest of their days in a second-best life, “plan B”, outside the place of God’s blessing.

With that picture in mind, every decision becomes an exam with no marks shown. Is this sense of peace from God, or from my own wishes? Was that verse this morning a sign? It is exhausting. And the fear can make us freeze, putting off decisions that need to be made, while life and other people wait.

The Bible names it

Scripture is honest about how little we can see. “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring” (Proverbs 27:1). Jeremiah confessed, “I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps” (Jeremiah 10:23). We are creatures. We do not hold the map of the future, and we were never meant to.

That limit is not the problem. The problem is what we do with it. Jesus spoke directly to the restless, future-gripping heart: “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matthew 6:34). The anxiety that grips us at a crossroads is often anxiety about tomorrow dressed in spiritual clothes. We say we are seeking God’s will. Often we are also trying to secure our future, and to make sure nothing goes wrong.

James describes a man who prays for wisdom and yet cannot settle: “the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind” (James 1:6). The cure James gives is not a cleverer method, but trust in a God “who gives generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5). We will come back to that promise.

Not a sign of a weak faith

If you feel this way, you are not strange, and you are not a poor Christian. Often the fear springs from something good: you take God seriously, and you want your life to honour him. Some of the most careful and conscientious believers suffer from it most. But good desires can be bent by false beliefs. Much of this study is about replacing those false beliefs with what God has actually said.

It may also help to know that Scripture is full of people who did not know what lay ahead. “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8). Abraham did not have the map. He had God, and God’s promise, and that was enough to walk on.

An example

A final-year student has offers from two universities for further study, one near home and one three hundred miles away. Both courses are good. She has prayed for weeks and asked God for a clear sign. She has made a spreadsheet, scored every factor, and found the totals almost equal. Each night she lies awake imagining the life she will miss if she chooses wrongly. Her friends have stopped asking. The deadline is a week away, and she feels further from an answer than when she began.

A better way

The good news is that God has not set us an exam with hidden answers. He is a Father, not a riddle-setter. He has made a great deal of his will plain, and he leads his children in ways that free them rather than freeze them. “I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you” (Psalm 32:8). The next chapters show how.

For reflection

Have you ever pictured God’s will as a single line you might step off? Where did that picture come from? Which decisions most easily freeze you: work, relationships, where to live, church? How much of your anxiety at a crossroads is really anxiety about tomorrow? What does it mean to you that Abraham “went out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8)?

2.title: The Will God Keeps and the Will God Gives
2.essay:
When Christians say “God’s will”, they can mean different things. Much of our anxiety comes from mixing them up. Scripture speaks of a will that God keeps to himself, and a will that he gives to us. Learning the difference is one of the most freeing things a worried believer can do.

The will God keeps: his decree

First, there is God’s sovereign plan, sometimes called his will of decree. God “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11). He is “declaring the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:10). He ordains whatever comes to pass, without being the author of sin, and his decree includes the means, so our choices and prayers are real.

So in one sense, yes, God does have a detailed plan for your life: “in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me” (Psalm 139:16). But notice two things about it. It cannot fail: you cannot step outside it, however hard you try. And it is hidden: you do not see it in advance. The study The Sovereignty of God explains this doctrine more fully.

The will God gives: his command

Second, there is God’s revealed will, sometimes called his will of command or precept. This is what he tells us to believe and do in Scripture. It can be disobeyed, and often is. But it is not hidden. It is written down, in plain words, for ordinary people.

Moses drew the line between the two: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29).

Here is the heart of the matter. The anxious Christian is usually trying to discover the secret will before acting. Scripture never asks us to do that. It asks us to obey the revealed will, and to trust God with the secret one.

What about a will of desire or direction?

Some speak of a third sense. Theologians often note that Scripture shows what pleases God even where he does not decree it: “Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23). This is sometimes called his will of desire or disposition. It belongs with his revealed will: it shows his heart, not a hidden plan for our choices.

Others speak of a will of direction: a specific, individual plan for each person’s choices, which God wants us to discover and which we can miss. The next chapter weighs that idea. But notice that Scripture never speaks of a third will that is both hidden and binding. What God has decreed, we cannot miss. What God has commanded, we can know.

What God has plainly said

So what has God revealed as his will for you? More than we often notice. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18).

Micah sums it up: “He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). “He has told you.” This is not a riddle.

And Paul gives the shape of the whole: “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect” (Romans 12:1–2). We discern God’s will not chiefly by receiving a message but by becoming a certain kind of person, given to God, with a mind made new. And it all begins “by the mercies of God”, with what Christ has already done.

Freedom inside the fence

Think of God’s commands as the fence round a wide field. Inside is a great deal of room. When Paul speaks to a widow about remarriage, he says she “is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). One boundary, and then freedom. On matters God has left open, “Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5).

So most of God’s will for your decision is already known. It is not mainly about where you will be, but who you will be there: holy, prayerful, thankful, just, kind and humble. You can obey that will in either town and in either job.

An example

A married couple in their fifties are weighing whether to move closer to their grandchildren. They have been asking God which choice is his will. One evening they write down everything Scripture plainly asks of them, whichever way they go: to love each other, to belong to a faithful church, to serve, to give, to honour an elderly mother who would stay behind. The list settles some questions at once. The choice that remains is smaller, and they find they can make it.

For reflection

Have you been trying to discover God’s secret will before you act? How does Deuteronomy 29:29 change that? Read 1 Thessalonians 4:3 and 5:16–18 and Micah 6:8. Which parts of God’s revealed will for you are already clear in your present decision? What would it mean to see God’s commands as a fence round a wide field?

3.title: Blueprints, Fleeces and Lots
3.essay:
Sincere Christians seek guidance in different ways. Some believe God has a specific plan for each choice that we must find. Some look for signs, or wait for an inner impression. Others say God’s word and wisdom are enough. These views deserve a fair hearing, and the stories Scripture tells deserve a careful reading.

The blueprint view

Many believers have been taught that God has an individual blueprint for every life: the right job, city and spouse. Our task is to discover it through prayer, Scripture, circumstances and an inner sense of God’s leading. Those who hold this view point to promises such as “I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go” (Psalm 32:8), and “your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, ‘This is the way, walk in it’” (Isaiah 30:21). At its best it guards a precious truth: God cares about the details of our lives.

The wisdom view

Others, such as Garry Friesen in Decision Making and the Will of God and Kevin DeYoung in Just Do Something, argue that Scripture speaks of God’s will only as his sovereign plan and his revealed commands. Within the commands, they say, God gives freedom and expects us to choose wisely, with prayer and counsel. They point out that Isaiah 30:21 is a promise to a people turning from idols back to God’s ways. They warn that the blueprint view breeds anxiety and passivity.

Impressions and signs

A third approach looks for God to speak directly: through an inner impression, a sense of peace, a dream, a fleece or a word from another believer. Many continuationist Christians believe God still gives prophecy, though they hold it is fallible and must be tested by Scripture. They would say they are simply expecting a living God to be personal.

Gideon’s fleece

Gideon is often held up as a model. But look at the story. God had already spoken. The angel told him, “Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?” (Judges 6:14). He had already received one sign. Then he laid out the fleece, saying, “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said” (Judges 6:36). He knew what God wanted. He was seeking reassurance, and then more: “Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece” (Judges 6:39).

God graciously answered a frightened man, which is a comfort to every weak believer. But the fleece is a picture of God’s patience with our doubts, not a method for discovering his plan. Jesus himself refused to put God to the test: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7).

Lots before Pentecost

When the apostles chose a replacement for Judas, they prayed and “cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias” (Acts 1:26). This was a lawful Old Testament practice: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). Acts does not criticise it. But it happened before Pentecost. After the Spirit was poured out, the church never cast lots again in the New Testament. When the apostles needed men to serve, they said, “pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom” (Acts 6:3). At the council of Jerusalem they reasoned from Scripture and wrote, “it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28).

Paul’s plans

Paul did receive extraordinary guidance. He was “forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia” and, after a vision of a man of Macedonia, his company went on, “concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them” (Acts 16:6–10). Such guidance came at turning points of the apostolic mission, as the study The Holy Spirit shows. But before the vision, Paul was making plans: “they attempted to go into Bithynia” (Acts 16:7).

That is how Paul usually decided. He prayed “that somehow by God’s will I may now at last succeed in coming to you”, and told the Romans he had “often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented)” (Romans 1:10–13). Weighing his own life and death, he reasoned his way to a conclusion: “Convinced of this, I know that I will remain” (Philippians 1:25).

James gives the right spirit: “Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit’, yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring … Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:13–15). James does not forbid planning. He forbids planning as if God were not King.

This commentary’s view

This commentary’s view: God guides his people chiefly through his word, prayer, wisdom and godly counsel, under his providence. Scripture is sufficient for faith and life, so no further revelation is needed, and the revealed gift of prophecy belonged to the church’s foundation. Believers should therefore not demand signs, cast lots or steer by dreams. Impressions may be real and God may use them, but they carry no authority of their own, must be weighed by Scripture and wisdom, and should never be presented as “God told me”. This commentary stands near the wisdom view, while gladly affirming the truth the blueprint view protects: God’s plan for us is detailed, personal and good, and he leads us in it, whether we can see it or not. We hold this charitably: many faithful believers seek guidance differently.

An example

A woman selling her flat sets a test: if it sells by the end of the month, she will move to the city; if not, she will stay. It sells on the last day, and she moves. Two years later she is unhappy and confused: had God not shown her? A wise friend helps her see that a sale is a sale, not a message, and that the real question had been whether the move was wise.

For reflection

Which of these three views is closest to what you were taught? What does Gideon’s fleece really show about God? Why might it matter that the lot was cast before Pentecost? How do Paul’s ordinary plans, and James 4:13–15, shape the way you plan?

4.title: What Lies Beneath
4.essay:
Why do decisions frighten us so much? Part of the answer is simply that we cannot see the future. But part of it lies deeper, in what our hearts are asking for. When we look honestly, we often find that we want something God has not promised, and are slow to trust what he has.

Wanting certainty more than God

Underneath many requests for guidance is a longing for certainty: to know, before I step, that this will turn out well. That longing is natural. But Scripture says, “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). God rarely gives us sight of the road ahead. He gives us himself. To demand a guarantee before we will move is, in the end, to ask to walk by sight. Often the question beneath the question is, “Can I avoid all risk?” The answer is no, and God loves us too much to pretend otherwise.

Wanting to be in control

A second desire is control. If I can find the right formula, the right verse, the right sign, then I can manage the outcome. This is close to the oldest temptation of all. The serpent told Eve that if she ate, “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). We want to know what only God knows. It is no accident that Scripture forbids every form of divination, fortune-telling and reading of omens (Deuteronomy 18:10–12).

When King Saul received no answer from God, he went to a medium: “Seek out for me a woman who is a medium, that I may go to her and inquire of her” (1 Samuel 28:7). His desperation to know the future led him away from God altogether. Our own methods are gentler. But opening the Bible at random, or treating every coincidence as a message, can come from the same restless need to know.

Wanting someone else to decide

Sometimes we want God to decide so that we will not be responsible. If the choice goes badly, at least it was not my fault. This can look like humility. But God made us to choose, with minds, desires and the call to act. The proverb warns, “Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered” (Proverbs 28:26). Notice that the alternative to trusting our own mind is not to stop thinking. It is to walk in wisdom.

The fear of being to blame often hides the fear of regret, or of what others will think. The studies Regret & the Past and The Fear of Man look at those struggles more closely.

Wanting a perfect life

Many of us have quietly made an idol of the ideal life: the career that fulfils, the marriage that never disappoints, the home in the right place. We then treat God’s will as the route to that life. If I choose correctly, everything will be well. So each choice carries the weight of our whole happiness. No wonder we tremble.

But God’s will for us is not first a comfortable life. It is likeness to his Son. Romans 8:28 is followed at once by the purpose behind it: to be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). God may lead us to that through ease or through hardship. A perfect life cannot be secured by perfect decisions. It is waiting for us in glory, and it is a gift.

Doubting the Father’s heart

At the bottom of it all is often a picture of God that is not true. We imagine him holding the answer behind his back, waiting to see whether we are spiritual enough to guess it. The serpent’s first words were a question about God’s goodness: “Did God actually say …?” (Genesis 3:1). He wanted Eve to think of God as withholding.

Jesus gives us a different picture: “If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:11). No good father sets his children a test and hides the answers. He teaches them, walks beside them and lets them grow. He is not waiting to catch them out.

An example

A man in his forties has talked for three years about leaving his job to train as a teacher. He keeps praying for a clear sign, and none comes. One day his wife asks gently, “What are you afraid of?” He realises the answer is not God at all. He is afraid that if it goes wrong, he will have no one to blame but himself. He has been waiting for God to take the risk for him. That honest moment does not make the decision, but it frees him to start thinking about it properly.

The mercy of being searched

It is not pleasant to see these things in ourselves. But God shows us our hearts in order to heal them. “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!” (Psalm 139:23–24). That last line is the prayer for guidance we most need: not first “show me which job”, but “lead me in the way everlasting”.

For reflection

Which of these desires do you recognise in yourself: certainty, control, avoiding blame or a perfect life? How does your picture of God shape the way you face decisions? What does Matthew 7:11 tell you about the Father you are asking? Pray Psalm 139:23–24, and listen.

5.title: Not My Will, but Yours
5.essay:
One night in a garden outside Jerusalem, the Son of God faced the greatest decision in the history of the world. He knew exactly what his Father’s will was, and it was the hardest thing ever asked of anyone. What he prayed there, and what he did next, changes how we face every decision of our own.

The garden

Jesus took Peter, James and John with him “and began to be greatly distressed and troubled” (Mark 14:33). He told them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Mark 14:34). Then he fell on the ground and prayed: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36). Luke records the words, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

Look at how he prays. He is completely honest. He tells his Father what he wants: that the cup would pass. He does not pretend to feel what he does not feel. And then he places his own desire under his Father’s will. The second time, the prayer has moved: “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (Matthew 26:42).

That is how a child of God prays at a crossroads. We may tell the Father exactly what we want. Then we place our wants in his hands.

Our situation is different

But notice the difference between Jesus and us. He knew the Father’s will precisely. The cup was the cross, the judgment of God against sin, which he would drink in our place. Our decisions are smaller, and usually we do not know which choice God has decreed. Yet Gethsemane teaches us that the hardest part of God’s will is rarely knowing it. It is trusting the Father enough to embrace it. Jesus did not need a sign. He needed, and had, perfect trust in his Father’s goodness.

And when he had prayed, he acted. “Rise, let us be going” (Matthew 26:46). Surrender did not make him passive. It sent him forward.

The will he embraced was for us

Here is the wonder. The will Jesus accepted in the garden was God’s will to save us. Isaiah had said it long before: “Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him” (Isaiah 53:10). Peter preached that Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23). And Hebrews says, “And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10).

So the deepest will of God for your life is not hidden at all. Jesus told us what it is: “this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6:40). Whatever you choose next month, that will stands.

Paul draws the conclusion that should quiet every anxious heart: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The Father who gave his Son for you is not hiding the path to watch you stumble.

Carried through our mistakes

What if we choose badly? Foolish choices have real consequences. But God’s providence is greater than our wisdom, and he weaves even our poor choices into his good purpose for his people. “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28).

Joseph’s brothers made a wicked choice. Joseph could say to them, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (Genesis 50:20). The book of Ruth begins with a family who left Bethlehem for Moab in a famine (Ruth 1:1). Many readers think that move was unwise, and it ended in grief. Yet through it a Moabite widow came to Bethlehem, married Boaz, and became great-grandmother to David (Ruth 4:17), and an ancestor of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).

Sometimes God simply redirects a good plan. David wanted to build a house for God, and even the prophet Nathan said, “Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you” (2 Samuel 7:3). That night God said no, and in the same breath promised, “the LORD will make you a house” (2 Samuel 7:11). David’s plan was not sin. God had something better.

The psalmist sums it up: “The steps of a man are established by the LORD, when he delights in his way; though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong, for the LORD upholds his hand” (Psalm 37:23–24).

An example

A nurse took a post overseas, convinced it was right. Within a year the hospital had closed and she came home, embarrassed and unsure what God was doing. She found a small church near her parents, where an older couple took her under their wing. Over the next years she learned to pray as she never had. But she has stopped calling it a mistake that put her outside God’s will. She calls it a chapter in a story her Father is still writing.

For reflection

What strikes you most about how Jesus prayed in Gethsemane? How does it help to know that the deepest will of God for you, your salvation in Christ, is not hidden? Where might God be weaving a poor choice of yours into something good? How does Romans 8:32 speak to your fear of choosing wrongly?

6.title: Making the Decision, and Afterwards
6.essay:
The truths of this study are meant for real decisions with real deadlines. Here are some practical steps for making a choice, and for living with it afterwards. They are not a formula that guarantees the right result. They are ways of walking with your Father, who has promised to lead you.

Start with what God has said

First ask: does Scripture settle this? Is one option sinful, or does one break a promise you have made, neglect your family or draw you away from Christ’s people? If so, you have your answer, and need no further guidance. “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). Then ask how each option would help you grow in holiness, love your neighbour and seek first his kingdom (Matthew 6:33).

Pray for wisdom

“If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (James 1:5). Notice the promise. God does not promise a voice or a sign. He promises wisdom, and he gives it without scolding us for asking. Tell him your hopes and fears, as Jesus did. “Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established” (Proverbs 16:3).

Think hard

Wisdom is not a feeling. It thinks. “The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps” (Proverbs 14:15). Gather the facts and count the cost, as a builder must (Luke 14:28). Write down what each option would mean for your faith, family, church and work. The study Biblical Wisdom shows how this kind of wisdom grows.

Ask others

“Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22). Talk to mature Christians who know you well: a pastor, older believers, your husband or wife, a trusted friend. Ask not only what they would do, but what they see in you.

Weigh desires, gifts and circumstances

Your own desires are not necessarily suspect. If your heart has been shaped by God, your longings matter. “Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 37:4). Weigh your gifts too: “As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another” (1 Peter 4:10). Take circumstances seriously too: doors open and closed, money, health, others’ needs. Read them humbly, as the setting God has given you, not as coded messages.

Decide, and say “if the Lord wills”

Then, within a sensible time, decide. “He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap” (Ecclesiastes 11:4). Choose freely within God’s commands, and hold the plan humbly: “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15). If both options are good, you are free to choose either. That is not failing to find God’s will. It is the freedom he gives.

Peace after deciding

Many Christians look for a feeling of peace to confirm a choice. Feelings are changeable, and Scripture does not treat them as God’s voice. The peace Scripture promises is deeper. “Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:6–7). It is the peace of a child who has left everything with his Father.

So when doubts come back after you have decided, do not keep digging up the seed to see if it is growing. If hard things follow, they are not proof that you chose wrongly: Paul knew suffering awaited him in Jerusalem, and his friends could only say, “Let the will of the Lord be done” (Acts 21:14). The study Disappointment & Waiting speaks to that experience. “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you” (Isaiah 26:3).

When indecision becomes something more

For some people, the fear of choosing wrongly becomes overwhelming: constant checking, endless reassurance-seeking, panic, or a dread that any choice might be sin. This can be a form of anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder, sometimes called scrupulosity. It is treatable. Seeing a doctor or a qualified counsellor is not a failure of faith, and medicine, where it is prescribed, is a good gift. The study Contentment & Anxiety says more.

If the decision you face is whether to leave a home where you are being harmed, do not wait for a sign. Safety comes first. Contact the police or emergency services if you are in danger, and tell a trusted person or your church leaders. And if the weight ever brings thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now: call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust. Your life is precious to God.

An example

A young couple have moved to a new town and visited three churches over two months. They feel stuck. One evening they sit down with a Bible and a sheet of paper. Which church preaches Christ faithfully from Scripture? Where could they serve, and be known? Two pass the test. They choose the nearer, commit, and stop comparing. A year later they cannot imagine being anywhere else, though they know they would have been cared for in the other church too.

Further reading

Kevin DeYoung’s Just Do Something is short, lively and freeing. Sinclair Ferguson’s Discovering God’s Will is a warm and careful treatment from a Reformed pastor.

You will face many more decisions. You will not always choose wisely, and you will never see far ahead. But the Shepherd goes before his sheep. “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want … He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake” (Psalm 23:1–3). You are not walking towards a test. You are walking home.

For reflection

Which of these steps do you most often skip? Who could you ask for counsel about the decision in front of you? What would it look like for you to decide, and then stop digging up the seed? How does knowing that the Shepherd goes before you change the way you face what is next?
